title: The People of Makkah Embrace Islam
subtitle: The Pledges of Mount Safa, the Conversion of Notable Adversaries, and Surah An-Nasr
summary: In the days following the general amnesty, thousands of citizens of Makkah climbed the slopes of Mount Safa to formally pledge their allegiance to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. From prominent aristocrats to former persecutors, the entire society embraced the faith in crowds, fulfilling the prophetic vision captured in Surah An-Nasr and permanently dissolving centuries of pagan tradition into the fraternity of Islam.

sections.text: Following the purification of the Kaaba and the proclamation of amnesty, the city of Makkah entered a profound spiritual metamorphosis. The idols that had anchored the civic and economic identity of Quraysh lay shattered in the dust, and the hearts of the people were melted by the Prophet's extraordinary mercy. On the morning following the conquest, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ took his seat upon the rocky knoll of Mount Safa to receive the formal oaths of allegiance (Bay'ah) from the men and women of Makkah.

Long lines of citizens climbed the slope of Safa, extending their hands to pledge their faith in Allah alone and their obedience to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in all righteous matters. The men pledged their commitment to uphold Islam, maintain the prayers, pay the Zakat, and defend the truth. Umar ibn al-Khattab sat below the Prophet, repeating the pledges aloud so that the vast gathering could hear.

When the men had completed their oaths, the women of Makkah assembled to take their pledge. In strict compliance with the Quranic instructions revealed in Surah Al-Mumtahanah, the Prophet accepted their allegiance upon moral and spiritual principles without physical contact:

يَا أَيُّهَا النَّبِيُّ إِذَا جَاءَكَ الْمُؤْمِنَاتُ يُبَايِعْنَكَ عَلَى أَنْ لَا يُشْرِكْنَ بِاللَّهِ شَيْئًا وَلَا يَسْرِقْنَ وَلَا يَزْنِينَ وَلَا يَقْتُلْنَ أَوْلَادَهُنَّ وَلَا يَأْتِينَ بِبُهْتَانٍ يَفْتَرِينَهُ بَيْنَ أَيْدِيهِنَّ وَأَرْجُلِهِنَّ وَلَا يَعْصِينَكَ فِي مَعْرُوفٍ فَبَايِعْهُنَّ
'O Prophet, when the believing women come to you pledging that they will not associate anything with Allah, nor steal, nor commit unlawful intercourse, nor kill their children, nor bring forth a slander they have fabricated, nor disobey you in what is right, then accept their pledge...' (Surah Al-Mumtahanah 60:12)

Among the women stood Hind bint Utbah, the wife of Abu Sufyan, who arrived veiled to conceal her identity out of shame for her past actions at Uhud. When the Prophet recited the condition: 'That you will not steal,' Hind interjected: 'O Messenger of Allah, Abu Sufyan is a frugal man, so I have taken from his household wealth without his knowledge.' The Prophet recognized her voice and smiled: 'Are you Hind bint Utbah?' She answered: 'Yes, O Messenger of Allah! Pardon what has passed, and may Allah pardon you!' The Prophet accepted her repentance warmly and confirmed her pledge, exemplifying the boundless capacity of Islam to erase all past errors.
The Moving Conversion of Abu Quhafa

Among the most deeply touching events of those days was the arrival of Abu Quhafa, the elderly, blind father of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq. Abu Bakr took his frail father by the hand and guided him gently through the crowd until he brought him before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, his hair and beard completely white like the blossoms of the thaghamah plant.
When the Prophet saw the frail elder standing before him, his heart was moved with profound tenderness. He turned to Abu Bakr and remarked with supreme reverence for age:

هَلاَّ تَرَكْتَ الشَّيْخَ فِي بَيْتِهِ حَتَّى أَكُونَ أَنَا آتِيهِ فِيهِ؟
'Why did you not leave the elder in his house so that I might come to him there?' (Musnad Ahmad; Al-Mustadrak by Al-Hakim)

Abu Bakr replied with filial devotion: 'O Messenger of Allah, it is more fitting that he should walk to you than you should walk to him.' The Prophet seated Abu Quhafa before him, placed his blessed hand upon the old man's chest, and invited him to faith. Abu Quhafa immediately recited the testimony of Islam. Abu Bakr wept tears of profound joy, thanking Allah that his father was guided to the light before his life reached its close.

In rapid succession, the leading figures who had anchored pagan resistance for decades—including Suhayl ibn Amr, Safwan ibn Umayyah, and Huwaytib ibn Abd al-Uzza—entered Islam with wholehearted conviction. The religious transformation of Makkah fulfilled the divine vision revealed in the beloved short chapter, Surah An-Nasr:

إِذَا جَاءَ نَصْرُ اللَّهِ وَالْفَتْحُ * وَرَأَيْتَ النَّاسَ يَدْخُلُونَ فِي دِينِ اللَّهِ أَفْوَاجًا * فَسَبِّحْ بِحَمْدِ رَبِّكَ وَاسْتَغْفِرْهُ إِنَّهُ كَانَ تَوَّابًا
'When the victory of Allah has come and the conquest, and you see the people entering into the religion of Allah in multitudes, then exalt [Him] with praise of your Lord and ask forgiveness of Him. Indeed, He is ever Accepting of repentance.' (Surah An-Nasr 110:1–3)

The capitulation of Makkah dissolved centuries of tribal idolatry across the Arabian Peninsula. Tribes from every corner of Arabia, who had long withheld judgment until the dispute between Quraysh and Muhammad was resolved, now realized that divine truth had definitively prevailed, paving the way for the historic delegations that would soon travel from across the peninsula to accept Islam.
